text: this is tfp photonics treams (see github). lets look into this a bit. also give me some idea on the complexity and size of the existing codebase

items.html:
It’s compact, mathematically dense scientific software. Making selected workflows differentiable looks quite tractable. Supporting everything treams supports is a substantially larger numerical-validation project.

I inspected treams at 1f5d0d6, plus the existing differentiable implementation.

[…] tfp-photonics/dreams […]. It contains spherical/core-shell T-matrices, multiple scattering, layered structures, and a differentiable 2D lattice-sum path.

Crucially, it already follows a hybrid approach: native special functions wrapped with custom derivatives, composed with JAX array operations. For example, Bessel, Hankel, and associated Legendre functions use pure_callback plus custom_jvp. Implementation.

How big is it?

These are my counts from the checked-out source: physical lines, including comments, docstrings, and blanks; excluding documentation, build files, and generated C.

Component Files Lines
treams Python source 13 8,714
treams Cython implementation 20 13,666
treams Cython declarations 13 329
treams total source 46 22,709
treams tests 16 6,005
dreams source 12 5,516
dreams tests 6 1,237

Treams contains 730 test-function definitions, versus 28 in dreams; these aren’t executed test-case counts or coverage measurements.

The source count also exaggerates the distinct implementation somewhat: 6,505 lines—29% of treams—sit in three files dominated by repetitive NumPy ufunc bindings and their documentation. That machinery wouldn’t necessarily survive a redesign. Source tree.

Where the complexity actually lives

Layer What makes it difficult
Multiple-scattering solve Relatively clean: assemble coupling matrices and solve a dense linear system.
Special functions and wave translations Complex-valued functions, recurrences, coordinate singularities, and polarization conventions.
Periodic lattice sums Ewald summation, convergence decisions, complex branches, and different dimensionalities. This is a substantial numerical component.
Public array API Custom NumPy dispatch propagates basis/material metadata. Convenient for users, but intrusive to retrofit for tracing.
Full feature coverage Cylindrical waves, arbitrary supplied T-matrices, band calculations, and numerical surface integration broaden the derivative contract.

These boundaries are visible in the interaction solve, lattice implementation, and array wrapper.

For the central solve, the derivative is particularly straightforward:

[ Ax=b \quad\Longrightarrow\quad dx=A^{-1}(db-dA,x). ]

That gives a natural custom-derivative boundary without differentiating the internals of a factorization. The harder work is obtaining accurate derivatives of the matrices being assembled.

[…]

Dreams also exposes concrete remaining scope: its periodic translation function defaults to a nondifferentiable sum path; the alternative is implemented for 2D, while 1D and 3D branches still call treams directly. That does not prevent every periodic optimization—for example, some parameters may leave the lattice coupling fixed—but it prevents claiming general differentiability. Periodic translation code.

And JAX here doesn’t imply fully GPU-native execution: its special-function callbacks execute on CPU, potentially introducing accelerator transfers and synchronization. JAX callback documentation.

For computational scale, (N) spheres at multipole order (L) give (D=2NL(L+2)) unknowns. The existing dense formulation has roughly (O(D^2)) storage and (O(D^3)) factorization cost: 100 spheres at (L=3) need about 144 MB per complex128 matrix; at (L=10), about 9.2 GB, before workspace and differentiation storage.

I’d start by identifying a useful workflow that dreams cannot currently differentiate. Extending that path looks like a credible side project. Full treams parity would mean preserving a considerable body of numerical behavior, even if the replacement code became much smaller.

This was source inspection and counting; I haven’t run either test suite or benchmarked performance. No source changes, pushes, or GitHub updates.

text: do you think it‘s possible to do a full rust reqrite while preserving today‘s python api? or making an even better python api

items.html:
Yes. A Rust numerical core with today’s Python API is entirely plausible. Based on the code we inspected, I’d be more concerned about reproducing numerical behavior than about Rust–Python integration.

The useful split would be:

  • Rust: special functions, wave translations, lattice sums, coefficient calculations, and numerical assembly.
  • Python: TMatrix, bases, materials, operators, and their user-facing behavior.
  • Existing linear algebra libraries: initially keep using established dense solvers.

That could preserve code such as:

tm = treams.TMatrix.cluster(spheres, positions).interaction.solve()

The Python classes would delegate numerical work to Rust. Preserving those classes initially also preserves much of the unusual NumPy dispatch and metadata propagation without having to reproduce it across a language boundary.

A literal rewrite of every layer into Rust is possible, but I don’t see much benefit in moving Python-specific API machinery there. Most of the interesting rewrite is in the numerical core anyway.

For a better Python API, I’d separate numerical arrays from the description of the problem more clearly. Currently, physical parameters and basis information travel through custom array wrappers. That’s convenient, but makes differentiation and interoperability harder.

An illustrative alternative:

system = SphereCluster(
    radii=radii,
    positions=positions,
    materials=materials,
    lmax=3,
)

result = system.solve(illumination)
result.scattering_cross_section()
result.electric_field(points)

Underneath, expose a small functional interface that accepts arrays and returns arrays. The friendly object API and the existing compatibility API could both use it. We’d need to trace actual workflows before deciding whether this is better than today’s conventions.

The important catch: a Rust rewrite does not itself deliver differentiability. We would still need derivative rules at the Python autodiff boundary and derivative implementations for the relevant Rust kernels. Likewise, CPU Rust kernels don’t automatically become GPU kernels. Those are separate design decisions.

I’d therefore distinguish three scopes:

Scope My assessment
Rust core, existing Python API Feasible and the lowest migration risk
Rust core, improved API alongside compatibility Feasible; probably the most useful destination
Full numerical parity, full differentiability, GPU support, redesigned API A substantial solver project

My preference would be a new Rust core behind the existing API first, with a simpler functional boundary designed for differentiation. Port one complete workflow—sphere cluster to observable and gradient—then expand. Today’s treams can serve as the reference throughout.

The size looks manageable. Matching conventions, convergence, singular limits, and complex-valued derivatives is where the effort will go.

text: generally i feel like when youre at the point where youre already implementing all the hard derivatives analyticslly, the value of autodiff frameworks really diminishes

items.html:
Yes—once the difficult numerical operations have analytic derivatives, the autodiff framework’s role becomes much narrower. It handles composition, bookkeeping, and user-defined objectives.

There’s still a meaningful distinction between implementing derivatives of individual kernels and implementing an end-to-end adjoint. If you provide derivatives for Bessel functions, translations, and lattice sums, someone still has to propagate sensitivities through matrix assembly, solves, illumination, and observables. Autodiff can do that composition. If you already implement that entire reverse pass yourself, much of its work is gone.

For treams, I think the strongest remaining reason is letting users construct objectives without deriving another adjoint:

loss = transmission(target_order) / total_transmission
loss += penalty(positions, radii)

The framework connects that objective—and possibly a user’s geometry parameterization—to the solver’s derivative interface.

That pushes me toward a Rust solver that owns its numerical derivatives and exposes vector–Jacobian products, with optional, thin adapters for autodiff frameworks. It should accept an output sensitivity and return parameter sensitivities without constructing a full Jacobian.

So I agree with your underlying point: the solver needn’t be written around an autodiff framework. The framework can sit at the boundary, where arbitrary user composition actually earns its place.

text: right. but assuming there is eg a rust solver, complete black box from python.. that just needs to implement a pullback for each exposed api no?

items.html:
Yes, exactly. For reverse-mode autodiff, each exposed differentiable operation needs a forward evaluation and a pullback:

outputs, context = rust.forward(inputs)
input_cotangents = rust.pullback(context, output_cotangents)

Python doesn’t need to see any internal computation. The context retains whatever the backward pass needs—such as the solution and matrix factorization.

And the boundary can be as coarse as you like. If one call maps geometry, materials, and illumination to observables, one pullback covers that entire solver call. You don’t need Python-visible derivative rules for its internal kernels.

Two qualifications:

  • Constructors, configuration, and discrete choices don’t need pullbacks. Only operations through which you want gradients.
  • The pullback must support arbitrary output cotangents, rather than only the gradient of one predefined objective. For complex arrays, the adapter also needs to match the framework’s conjugation convention.

Then the framework simply connects your solver’s pullback to the user’s parameterization and objective. That’s precisely the architecture you’re describing, and my previous answer overstated how much integration was necessary.

text: advect has a bunch of features that make it nice for agents to use and discover. what are those?
while youre doing that - explain what was implement wrt wasm and gpu

items.html: Advect’s useful agent features include versioned Markdown docs, a queryable support catalog, detailed local help() contracts, repair-oriented errors, and public gradient-checking utilities. Its compatibility tables and machine-readable docs are generated and checked, which helps keep discovery consistent with the implementation.

Advect has several concrete features that help agents discover capabilities, write correct code, and diagnose mistakes:

  • An agent-readable documentation index: llms.txt links to version-matched Markdown pages with expanded API signatures, docstrings, and examples. The homepage advertises it for automated discovery.
  • A live capability catalog: ad.support_catalog() reports supported operations, dynamic/staged/serialized execution, and JVP/VJP capabilities. Compatibility tables are generated from this data. I confirmed the installed 0.2.0 package exposes it. Source
  • Useful local introspection: help(), signatures, docstrings, and dir(advect) expose the public API—including lazily loaded functions—without requiring web access. Package entry point
  • Actionable diagnostics: errors carry operation names, reasons, and source locations; missing derivative rules include implementation examples. Debug mode identifies nonfinite values with shape, dtype, and bounded previews. Errors
  • Public correctness checks: check_gradient() validates composed derivatives; check_primitive() checks a custom operation’s promised capabilities. Testing utilities
  • Executable documentation: browser examples run the actual Advect wheel, automatically execute prerequisite snippets, and are checked in native/Pyodide CI. Documentation guide
  • Explicit contributor routing: scoped AGENTS.md files identify ownership, boundaries, required reading, and verification commands. Repository guidance

For treams-rs WASM, the complete Rust core now compiles to WebAssembly. A dedicated JavaScript/TypeScript interface exposes layered/chiral spheres, interacting sphere clusters, repeated illumination, and exterior electric fields. It runs entirely in the browser, without Python or a server. The module is 493 kB, or 177 kB gzip, excluding JavaScript glue, and was numerically checked in Node and Chrome. It currently runs serially and exposes a subset of the Python API: no browser adjoints, periodic systems, internal fields, or WebGPU. Its cluster constructor still builds the full dense T-matrix. WASM details

For GPU, there are two explicitly enabled native backends:

Path Implemented Measured on the 4080 SUPER
Dense algebra Complex128 cuBLAS/cuSOLVER operations, resident matrices, reusable LU factors, normal/adjoint solves, and solve pullbacks Mixed: large factor-and-solve 1.14×, some resident products 2.02×; CPU wins repeated triangular solves
cuTile fields Pure-Rust weighted plane-wave evaluation at requested points, retaining mode data on-device and avoiding a point-by-mode matrix 1.41–2.65×, including transfers after warmup; initial JIT approximately 0.5 s

Both share numerical conventions and relevant mathematics with the CPU core, and compile out of default builds. GPU fields currently have no pullback. This CUDA support is separate from browser WASM execution. GPU implementation and benchmarks

items.html:
I’d make a small, beautifully presented collection of experiments, each built around something you can discover with your fingers. My favourites for the first version are moving particles to shape light and finding resonances in a single sphere.

  1. Move the particles, shape the light

    Two spheres sit in an animated field. Drag them closer, change their sizes, or rotate the illumination arrow. Watch the interference pattern and the field between them change.

    A press-and-hold comparison shows what changes when the particles scatter off each other. Small challenges could be “make the brightest gap” or “make the field at this marker disappear.”

    This would be the flagship: immediately playful, while teaching the multiple scattering central to treams. The existing cluster example provides the underlying physics.

  2. Find a resonance

    A sphere, a field picture, and a small spectrum along the bottom. Scrub through wavelength; tap a peak to inspect it. Changing the radius moves the resonances.

    Reveal dipole, quadrupole, and higher-order contributions as selectable layers. You can see when a simple dipole approximation works and when it misses the interesting behaviour. This naturally extends the single-sphere example.

    This is probably the strongest combination of visual appeal, teaching value, and manageable mobile computation.

  3. Mix the waves

    A few incoming modes have amplitude sliders and phase dials. Blend them and watch the incident and scattered fields change.

    Beneath the picture, a compact animated diagram shows incoming coefficients → T-matrix → outgoing coefficients, with the equation (b=Ta) available on tap. It makes the central abstraction tangible: the object stays fixed while you change how you illuminate it.

    I’d start with one sphere and only three or four modes.

  4. Make a particle scatter less

    Add a shell around a sphere. Drag its thickness and adjust its optical properties to reduce scattering at a chosen wavelength.

    Show the original and coated responses using the same colour scale, plus a scattering score. Then change wavelength and discover how narrow the improvement might be.

    This gives the layered-sphere capability a clear purpose and introduces cancellation and design trade-offs.

  5. Left-handed and right-handed light

    Illuminate a materially chiral sphere and flip the light’s handedness with a large toggle. A small rotating vector illustrates polarization; the field and scattering response show its consequences.

    Flip the material’s chirality and compare again. It would showcase a distinctive treams capability through a simple interaction.

  6. Tap a target; let the solver improve the design

    Place a target outside a small particle cluster, then press Improve. Watch particle positions or radii change to increase the field there. Show sensitivity arrows before each step.

    This would be a compelling adjoint demonstration. It comes later: native derivatives exist, but we still need to expose their retained state and pullbacks through WASM.

For mobile, I’d give these a consistent visual language:

  • A large field canvas, crisp particle outlines, restrained colours, and a visible scale.
  • Direct manipulation, with two or three primary controls in a bottom sheet.
  • One useful starting configuration; Reset, Compare, and Why does this happen? always easy to reach.
  • A 2D slice through the 3D simulation as the default view.
  • Shareable configurations, so an interesting discovery becomes a link.

The responsiveness trick is to animate harmonic phase from the cached complex field. Recompute when parameters change, use a coarser preview while dragging, and refine after release. That gives us a good route to fluid interaction without solving every animation frame.

The first five mostly use mathematics already exposed or available behind small WASM helpers. We’d need a few careful additions for comparisons and observables, and actual phone profiling before choosing the final particle counts and field resolution.
